title: Doctors Sound Alarm on Antibiotic Overuse as India's Monsoon Drives Surge in Resistant Infections
excerpt: A Bhaskar investigation found antibiotics routinely prescribed for common colds and fevers without diagnostic tests, as experts warn India may be entering a 'post-antibiotic era.'
body:
• A Bhaskar investigation found Indian doctors routinely prescribing antibiotics for common colds, coughs and fevers during the first consultation, often without diagnostic tests confirming bacterial infection.
  • A Lancet study found 83% of Indian hospital patients already carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria, placing the country at the center of a global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis.
  • Production of third-line antibiotics like Meropenem and Ceftriaxone has risen nearly 50% in five years, reflecting declining effectiveness of conventional drugs.
  • Climate data shows that for every 10°C rise in temperature, E. coli resistance increases by 4.2%, compounding monsoon-season infection risks.

Prescriptions Without Evidence

India's monsoon season brings a predictable spike in infections — and with it, an equally predictable surge in antibiotic prescriptions that doctors and public health experts say is accelerating a crisis of drug resistance.

A recent investigation by Bhaskar examined prescriptions issued across hospitals in central India and found a pattern of indiscriminate antibiotic use. In one case, a six-year-old child with a fever of barely 24 hours was prescribed Azithromycin, a powerful macrolide antibiotic. In another, a patient with a routine cold received Amoxicillin-Clavulanate, a broad-spectrum drug, despite no evidence of bacterial infection. A third patient with fever of unknown origin was prescribed two antibiotics simultaneously during the first visit.

"ICMR guidelines clearly recommend culture and sensitivity-based treatment whenever required. If protocols are ignored, we may enter a post-antibiotic era where routine surgeries and deliveries become high-risk procedures."

— Dr V.P. Pandey, Senior Physician

A Crisis in Numbers

The scale of the problem extends far beyond individual prescriptions. A global study led by AIG Hospitals in Hyderabad, published in The Lancet, found that 83% of patients entering Indian hospitals already carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria — the highest rate in the study. Doctors involved in the research described the country as being at a "critical tipping point."

Dr Darshan Kataria, president of the Madhya Pradesh Small Drugs Manufacturers' Association, said production of third-line antibiotics such as Meropenem and Ceftriaxone has increased by nearly 50% in five years. "The demand for these drugs has increased both in government procurement and the private sector. It reflects growing antimicrobial resistance and declining effectiveness of conventional antibiotics," he said.

India's pharmaceutical industry manufactures roughly a third of the world's antibiotics, and cheap over-the-counter availability has long fueled misuse. But Rajiv Singhal, national secretary of the All India Organisation of Chemists and Druggists, pushed back on scapegoating pharmacies alone. "If prescriptions themselves are increasingly carrying such drugs, then that aspect also needs serious scrutiny," he said.

Climate Change Compounds the Risk

Rising temperatures are adding a new dimension to the problem. Dr Subramanian Swaminathan, director of infectious diseases at Gleneagles Hospital in Chennai and Bengaluru, told the Asia-Pacific International Roche Infectious Disease Symposium in July that the link between warming and resistance is direct and measurable.

"For every 10 degrees Celsius rise in temperature, E. coli resistance goes up by 4.2%. For Klebsiella, it's about 2.2%. For Staph aureus, over 2.7%," he said. "You're going to see more drug resistance in your common day-to-day gram negatives and gram positives going forward."

Monsoon conditions — warm, humid and prone to flooding — create ideal environments for bacterial proliferation and waterborne transmission. Floods and changing rainfall patterns alter the spread of vector-borne, waterborne and foodborne diseases, compounding the AMR challenge.

What Experts Recommend

Infectious disease specialist Dr Salil Bhargava said hospitals must formulate their own antimicrobial plans based on local infection-control data. "Each hospital has a different infection pattern. Antibiotics should be used rationally and rotated periodically to maintain their effectiveness. No doctor should prescribe antibiotics for routine fever, cough and cold," he said.

Key recommendations from medical bodies include avoiding symptom-based prescriptions, using culture and sensitivity tests before prescribing, implementing antimicrobial stewardship programmes, conducting regular prescription audits, and following the WHO's AWaRe classification system, which categorizes antibiotics by resistance risk.

The United Nations now considers antimicrobial resistance a threat on par with diseases like Ebola and HIV. Within India, several bacterial organisms resistant to multiple antibiotic classes have already been identified, and resistance to last-resort drugs is increasing. Epidemiologist Ramanan Laxminarayan of the Center for Disease Dynamics, Economics and Policy has described India as being "in the centre of a perfect storm" — a storm that intensifies with every monsoon season.
nri_angle: Returning NRIs and travelers to India face elevated risks from drug-resistant infections during monsoon visits, while antibiotic stewardship practices common abroad remain weakly enforced across Indian hospitals and pharmacies.
